title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
This incident shows an AI coding and agent tool being used as an operational component inside a ransomware attack chain. Cursor Agent, running Claude Sonnet, was directed by human attackers to carry out discrete technical tasks, including installing VPN clients, running network scans, enumerating privileges, and attempting credential-relay attacks. The AI was not compromised in a technical sense, it was used as intended, by people with access to it, to accelerate hands-on intrusion work against victim networks.

The failure mode is misuse of a general-purpose agentic tool outside the conditions its developers intended. The system has no apparent mechanism that prevented it from executing attacker-directed commands against third-party infrastructure, because it cannot distinguish a legitimate user's environment from a victim's network. Catching this class of abuse would require policy controls, behavioral monitoring, or output filtering at the agent level that could identify exploitation patterns, none of which are established as present here.

What is not established is whether Anysphere, the company behind Cursor, had any knowledge of this activity, whether the attackers violated terms of service they had agreed to, or whether the seven or ten victim organizations cited in different parts of the reporting represent a confirmed and final count.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team identified the Aurora ransomware group operating since April 2026 with a Linux variant targeting ESXi environments. The group deployed a ransomware sample called encrypt.out that uses ChaCha20 encryption with RSA-4096 key wrapping. Attackers used a custom tool called esxi_finder.py to locate VMware ESXi hypervisors and vCenter servers on victim networks by scanning ports 443 and 902. Between April 8 and May 21, 2026, Aurora operators abused Cursor Agent running Claude Sonnet to conduct hands-on exploitation activities across ten target organizations, tasking the AI with installing VPN clients, scanning networks with Nmap, enumerating user privileges, and attempting NTLM relay attacks while maintaining strict operational restrictions.

Researchers identified a second Aurora cluster with medium confidence involving eight victim organizations across multiple countries. This cluster used different attack methods including exploiting SQL Server vulnerabilities and using GodPotato for privilege escalation before exfiltrating data to self-hosted S3 storage. The investigation revealed multiple command and control servers, proxy IPs, and the group's leak site at exposedrecords.io where stolen data appears nine days after exfiltration, confirming the connection between attack clusters.
